data.title: Freckles (ephelides) — viva
data.summary: Pigmentary disorders · 15 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Freckles (ephelides)** (Pigmentary disorders)_

**Q1. What are freckles?**
- Small (1–5 mm) light-brown/red-brown macules on sun-exposed skin of fair-skinned (Fitzpatrick I–II) individuals; appear in early childhood (~age 3), darken in summer and fade in winter
- Strongly associated with red hair/ MC1R variants (red hair colour alleles) — markers of UV sensitivity and melanoma risk

**Q2. Histopathology.**
- Increased melanin in basal keratinocytes with normal number of melanocytes (which are larger and more active); no elongation of rete ridges — unlike lentigo

**Q3. Differentiate freckles from lentigines.**
- Freckles: childhood onset, sun-dependent (fade in winter), sun-exposed sites only, lighter colour, normal melanocyte number, no rete elongation
- Lentigines: any age, not sun-dependent, can be on any site including mucosa, darker, increased melanocytes along basal layer, elongated rete ridges

**Q4. Associations.**
- Axillary/inguinal freckling (Crowe's sign — NF1), xeroderma pigmentosum (freckling in first years of life with marked photosensitivity), Peutz–Jeghers (perioral lentigines — not true freckles), LEOPARD/Noonan with multiple lentigines

**Q5. Management.**
- Reassurance — benign; photoprotection (broad-spectrum sunscreen, clothing) — also reduces skin cancer risk; counsel skin self-examination in fair, freckled individuals
- Cosmetic: hydroquinone/azelaic acid, chemical peels, cryotherapy, Q-switched/picosecond lasers, IPL — recurrence with sun exposure

**Q6. Why do freckles darken in summer? Explain at cell level.**
- UV upregulates POMC/α-MSH and MC1R signalling → more tyrosinase activity and larger, more numerous eumelanin/pheomelanin melanosomes transferred to keratinocytes; melanocyte number is not increased, so pigment fades when UV stimulus falls in winter

**Q7. What is the role of MC1R?**
- Melanocortin-1 receptor on melanocytes; α-MSH binding raises cAMP → eumelanin synthesis
- Loss-of-function variants (R151C, R160W, D294H — 'red hair colour' alleles) give red hair, fair skin, freckling, poor tanning and higher melanoma and NMSC risk independent of UV

**Q8. Dermoscopy of a freckle?**
- Light-brown homogeneous or faint reticular pattern with sharp moth-eaten border; no globules or dots — helps distinguish from naevi

**Q9. What is the significance of freckling in xeroderma pigmentosum?**
- Freckle-like pigmentation in the first 1–2 years of life with severe sunburn on minimal exposure; followed by poikiloderma, actinic keratoses and skin cancers in the first decade — DNA repair (NER) defect; needs strict photoprotection

**Q10. Freckles and skin cancer risk — counselling.**
- Freckling (especially with red hair, blue eyes, poor tanning) is an independent risk factor for melanoma and non-melanoma skin cancer — counsel sunscreen, shade, clothing, avoid sunburn and tanning beds, regular skin self-examination

**Q11. What is the Fitzpatrick skin type classification?**
- I always burns never tans; II usually burns tans minimally; III sometimes burns tans gradually; IV burns minimally tans well (most North Indians); V rarely burns tans profusely (South Indians); VI never burns deeply pigmented — guides phototherapy dosing and laser settings

**Q12. What is the UV index and photoprotection advice?**
- UV index ≥3 — protection needed; avoid 10 am–4 pm sun, seek shade, protective clothing (UPF ≥30), wide-brimmed hat, broad-spectrum SPF ≥30 sunscreen 2 mg/cm² reapplied every 2 h, sunglasses

**Q13. Classify sunscreens (PYQ: classify sunscreens).**
- Organic (chemical) UV absorbers: UVB — PABA derivatives, cinnamates (octinoxate), salicylates, octocrylene; UVA — benzophenones (oxybenzone), avobenzone, ecamsule, newer broad-spectrum (bemotrizinol/ Tinosorb S, bisoctrizole/ Tinosorb M)
- Inorganic (physical) blockers: zinc oxide, titanium dioxide (micronised/ nano); iron oxides for visible light
- Ideal sunscreen: broad spectrum UVA+UVB, photostable, water-resistant, cosmetically acceptable, non-irritant, non-comedogenic

**Q14. What is SPF and PA?**
- SPF = MED with sunscreen / MED without (UVB protection) at 2 mg/cm² application; SPF 30 blocks ~97% UVB
- PA (+ to ++++) grading by persistent pigment darkening (UVA protection factor); UVA-PF ≥1/3 of SPF for 'broad spectrum' (EU)

**Q15. How does Wood's lamp help in pigmentary disorders?**
- 365 nm UVA absorbed by epidermal melanin: epidermal hyperpigmentation is accentuated (melasma epidermal type, freckles, CALM), dermal pigment is not; depigmentation (vitiligo, piebaldism) shows bright chalk-white; hypopigmentation (nevus depigmentosus, PA, IGH) shows dull off-white; also fluorescence of infections (PV yellow, erythrasma coral-red)

## Quick spotter facts
- Sun-exposed tiny brown macules darkening in summer in fair child — freckles
- Axillary freckling — NF1

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (Hypermelanoses). Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
